opus-5.5.text:
So the core issue is that neural networks are trying to represent far more concepts than they have neurons. If you've got, say, a few thousand neurons in a layer but the model needs to know about millions of concepts, like the Golden Gate Bridge, legal reasoning, the color blue, or deception, it can't give each one its own dedicated neuron. So it compresses them. Each neuron ends up participating in lots of different concepts, and each concept is spread across lots of neurons. That's superposition. It's very efficient for the model, but it's terrible for us, because when you look at any single neuron it's a jumble.

What an interpreter model does, and the classic version is something like a sparse autoencoder, is learn to take those dense, tangled activations and project them out into a much larger space, where each direction ideally corresponds to one clean, human-understandable concept. You're essentially expanding the representation back out. Instead of four thousand neurons that each mean fifty things, you get maybe hundreds of thousands or millions of features that each mean roughly one thing. And critically, only a handful of those features are active at any given time, which is the sparsity part. That's what makes it legible.

The important thing to understand is that we're not changing the underlying model when we do this. The superposition is still there inside the network; the model keeps computing the way it always has. What we've built is more like a lens, or a decoder ring. We read the model's internal state, translate it into this unscrambled feature space, and then we can say, okay, right now the model is thinking about this concept and that concept.

And where it gets really exciting is that it works in both directions. Once you know which direction in activation space corresponds to a given concept, you can intervene. You can turn a feature up or down and write that back into the model, and see how the behavior changes. That's how you go from just observing the model to actually understanding causally what each concept is doing, and eventually to designing and editing models more precisely, rather than just training them and hoping for the best.

It isn't perfect. There's reconstruction error, some features are still a bit muddy or split in odd ways, and there's real debate about whether the features we find are the model's true units of computation or just a convenient basis for us. But even with those caveats, it's been a huge step from staring at an incomprehensible soup of neurons to having something you can actually read and work with.

r001.rationale: The response explains superposition and describes unscrambling concepts, but it does not present that recovery as evidence that the base model’s superposition was real.

r002.rationale: It says interpreter features ideally correspond to one clean concept and that only a handful are active at a time, describing clean, sparse units.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the superposition remains inside the network and the interpreter only reads and translates its internal state.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that superposition is really a compression problem. A model has far more concepts it wants to represent than it has neurons or dimensions to represent them in, so it packs them in. It stores many features in the same directions, overlapping, kind of like how you can store more vectors than dimensions if you're willing to tolerate a little interference between them. And that's why when you look at a single neuron in a frontier model, it's polysemantic. It fires on something about DNA sequences, and also legal language, and also a certain kind of Python syntax, and there's no clean story.

So what an interpreter model does, and this is what we're building at Goodfire, is essentially learn to undo that compression. You train something like a sparse autoencoder, or a transcoder, or whatever the architecture is, to take those dense superposed activations and project them into a much higher-dimensional space where each direction, each feature, ideally corresponds to one human-interpretable concept. You're trading dimensions for sparsity. Only a handful of features are active for any given token, and that sparsity is what lets the concepts separate.

Now, how do you actually understand what happened? There are a few things we look at. One is reconstruction. If you take the features, push them back through the decoder, and recover the original activations, how much of the model's behavior did you preserve? If you swap the real activations for the reconstructed ones and the model's loss barely moves, you've captured most of what was there. If it degrades a lot, the interpreter is leaving stuff on the table, and that stuff is often the hard-to-disentangle, dense part that's still sitting in superposition.

The second thing is you look at the geometry of the features you've pulled out. If the interpreter has done its job, features that the base model had crammed into nearly the same direction now live in distinct, mostly orthogonal slots, and you can see which ones were interfering with each other. That's actually really informative, because the interference structure tells you something about what the model considered "safe" to overlap. It tends to overlap things that rarely co-occur.

And then the third thing, which I think is underrated, is you intervene. You don't just read the features, you steer them. You amplify one, suppress another, and watch what the model does. If turning up a feature you've labeled "formality" makes the output more formal and nothing else changes, that's strong evidence you've actually isolated the concept rather than some entangled bundle. If it drags three other behaviors along with it, you've learned that your decomposition is still partially superposed.

The honest caveat is that the interpreter model is itself a model, and it has its own failure modes. It can split one concept into many features because of how it was trained, or merge things that should be separate. So we spend a lot of time on evaluations, on asking whether the features are useful for a downstream task like detecting a specific behavior or editing it, rather than just whether they look nice. "Does it work" is a better test than "does it look interpretable."

r001.rationale: The response describes concepts as packed into shared directions, then says the interpreter separates them into distinct features, revealing which ones interfered.

r002.rationale: It describes an ideal representation with one feature per human-interpretable concept, only a handful active per token, and explicitly calls this sparse.

r003.rationale: It says uncaptured dense activations remain in superposition and that a decomposition can still be partially superposed after interpretation.

astra-6.text:
I think of it less as removing superposition from the network and more as finding a representation that makes it easier for us to understand. The network is still doing its computation in the original, compressed representation, where different features can share the same neurons or directions.

An interpreter model tries to unpack that into a larger set of features, ideally with only a small number active for any particular input. So you’re moving from a dense, overlapping representation to something sparse and more legible.

But that doesn’t guarantee you’ve recovered the network’s true concepts. There may be multiple ways to explain the same activations, and the interpreter can split features, combine them, or miss something. The stronger test is whether those features help you predict—and, through interventions, explain—the network’s behavior.

r001.rationale: The response describes an interpreter unpacking features, but does not say that recovering disentangled concepts is evidence the base model’s superposition was real.

r002.rationale: It says the interpreter aims for sparse, legible features, but does not state that concepts are represented in theoretically clean, sparse units.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the base network continues computing in its original compressed representation, where features share neurons or directions, after the interpreter unpacks them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a change of coordinates. The network has more concepts than it has dimensions to represent them, so those concepts share dimensions—that’s superposition. An interpreter model tries to recover a set of features that makes that representation easier for us to understand.

For example, a sparse autoencoder maps the network’s activations into a larger space where relatively few features are active at once. The hope is that those features correspond more closely to individual concepts. But it hasn’t removed superposition from the original network; it’s learned a way to describe what’s there. And that description isn’t necessarily unique or complete. You still have to test whether the recovered features actually explain the network’s behavior.

r001.rationale: The response explains that concepts share dimensions, but does not treat recovering features as evidence that the base model’s superposition was real.

r002.rationale: It says sparse autoencoders aim for relatively few active features and that features may correspond more closely to concepts; it does not describe them as theoretically clean, sparse units.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly says the interpreter has not removed superposition from the original network.
